Source Length

Watch Frontend vs Backend · Ahmed Mahmoud 7 min

Task · Get set up

  1. Install VS Code, Chrome, Git, and Node.js LTS.
  2. VS Code extensions: Live Server, Prettier, Error Lens, Auto Rename Tag.
  3. Create a GitHub account with a professional username.
  4. In week-0.md, explain in 10-15 lines, in your own words: what happens between typing facebook.com and seeing the page? No AI.
  5. Open any site, edit some text through DevTools → Elements, take a screenshot.

Submit your GitHub profile link, the file, and the screenshot on the dashboard.

Bonus: open DevTools → Network and refresh a site. How many requests? What's the biggest file? Which file types did you see?

How to ask a good technical question
  1. Read the error. Most of the time the answer is in it.
  2. Search the exact error message.
  3. Try for 20-30 minutes, then ask. Don't stay stuck for 3 days.
  4. When you ask, include what you wanted, what you did, what happened, and the code and error as text, not a phone photo of your screen.

Don't spend a week picking themes and installing 40 extensions. Set up the basics and start.

Mentor tip: consistency beats talent. One hour a day beats seven hours on Friday. Missed a week? Don't restart. Continue from where you are.
checklist: I can explain Frontend vs Backend to a non-programmer
I know what Client, Server, Request, and Response mean
I know what DNS does and why we need it
I can navigate folders and create files from the terminal
I can open DevTools, edit the page, and read the Console
VS Code is set up and Live Server works

1.body:
Task · About Me page

Build index.html about yourself. HTML only, no CSS.

  • Your name in an h1 and a short bio
  • A photo with a meaningful alt
  • A list of hobbies and a numbered list of this year's goals
  • A table of your weekly study schedule
  • Links to your GitHub and LinkedIn that open in a new tab
  • A second page, hobbies.html, linked both ways

Bonus: use colspan and rowspan to rebuild your college timetable.

Pitfalls: <br> for spacing (that's CSS's job) · picking headings by size instead of meaning (one h1 per page) · closing tags in the wrong order.

Mentor tip: don't memorize tags. Write a lot and they stick. Forgot one? Open MDN. Senior devs do it every day.
checklist: I know the difference between an element, a tag, and an attribute
I know why alt matters, and not just for SEO

Task · Event sign-up form

A sign-up page for a CIS workshop or hackathon:

Task · Profile card

Turn your week 1 page into a centered profile card:

  • A separate CSS file, no inline style=""

5.body:
Task · Dashboard layout

Layout only, no functionality needed:

  • Sidebar, header, and main area with grid-template-areas
  • Main area: 4 stat cards, one wide "chart" card spanning 2 columns, and a "Recent activity" card
  • Stat cards auto-flow with repeat(auto-fit, minmax(200px, 1fr))
  • A pure-CSS loading spinner (@keyframes)
  • Cards lift on hover with transform

Bonus: a flip card that turns over on hover (3D transforms + backface-visibility).

Pitfalls: using only Grid or only Flex. Rule of thumb: Grid for page layout, Flex for components. Too much animation annoys people, and some get physically uncomfortable.

Mentor tip: see a site you like? Open DevTools and see how its layout is built. You'll learn more than from any course.

7.body:
Tailwind doesn't replace knowing CSS. Every class is a CSS line you already know. If flex justify-between items-center isn't obvious to you, go back to week 4.

You need Node.js LTS to run Vite. Just follow the install steps for now; npm and Vite get a full week in week 16.

Task · Pricing page in Tailwind + dark mode

  • Rebuild your week 4 navbar + pricing cards from scratch in Tailwind
  • Fully responsive
  • A dark mode toggle (dark: + one line of JS: document.documentElement.classList.toggle('dark'))
  • Custom colors in @theme
  • Deploy on Vercel or Netlify. GitHub Pages needs extra setup with Vite.

Bonus: compare the final CSS file size of the Tailwind version and your plain CSS version. Which is smaller, and why?

Pitfalls: dynamic class names like `bg-${color}-500` (Tailwind can't see them) · @apply everywhere, which is just plain CSS the hard way.

Mentor tip: install the Tailwind CSS IntelliSense extension. It halves the time you spend hunting for class names.

8.title: Project 1: Landing Page
8.body:
Goal: build a real landing page from a design, alone, with no video to follow. Just you and the design.

Pick one:

  • A Junior or Intermediate landing page on Frontend Mentor
  • A landing page from Figma Community with mobile and desktop frames
Requirement Details
Sections 5+: navbar, hero, features, testimonials or pricing, footer
Responsive Mobile first; works at 375 px, 768 px, and 1440 px
Semantic HTML Right tags, one h1
Accessibility alt everywhere, keyboard-friendly, readable contrast
Styling Plain CSS or Tailwind, your call
Git 10+ meaningful commits, none called final
Deploy Live on GitHub Pages, Vercel, or Netlify
README Screenshot, live link, tools used, hardest part
Lighthouse 90+ in Accessibility and Best Practices

Mentor tip: this is the first thing in your portfolio. Build it like someone is paying you. Then have a friend open it on their phone and tell you the truth.

9.body:
Task · Problem set

In week-9.js, one function per problem, results printed to the Console:

  1. BMI from weight and height, with a category
  2. Even or odd, with an error message for non-numbers
  3. Largest of three without Math.max
  4. Celsius ↔ Fahrenheit
  5. Letter grade (A-F) from a score, using switch
  6. Palindrome check (level, racecar)
  7. Capitalize "hello world" → "Hello World"

Bonus: a number-guessing game with prompt and alert. The computer picks 1-100 and answers "higher" or "lower". You'll need a loop, so peek at the first loops video.

Pitfalls: watching without typing (JS can't be learned by watching) · ignoring red in the Console. An error is a message telling you exactly where to look.

Mentor tip: this week looks easy. Don't rush it. Type coercion and falsy values are behind half the weird bugs you'll ever hit.

10.body:
Task · Grade calculator

An array of 10 students, each [name, grade]. Write:

  1. getAverage(students)
  2. getTopStudent(students)
  3. getFailed(students): grades under 50
  4. sortByGrade(students): descending, without mutating the original
  5. printReport(students): a nicely formatted Console report with grades and letters

No map, filter, or reduce yet. Loops only.

Bonus: print a star pyramid with any number of rows.

   *
  ***
 *****

Pitfalls: functions that do five things · a missing return, so you get undefined · names like x, arr, temp.

Mentor tip: wrote the same code twice? It should be a function.

11.body:
Task · Student data analysis

const students = [
  { id: 1, name: "Ahmed", age: 20, track: "frontend", grades: [85, 90, 78], active: true },
  { id: 2, name: "Sara", age: 21, track: "backend", grades: [92, 88, 95], active: true },
  { id: 3, name: "Omar", age: 19, track: "frontend", grades: [60, 45, 70], active: false },
  // ...15 students total
];

Using only map, filter, reduce (no plain loops):

  1. Names of active students
  2. Each student with an average field (new objects)
  3. Count per track { frontend: 6, backend: 5 } with reduce
  4. Top student per track
  5. A greeting function that destructures { name, track } in its parameters
  6. Add a student without mutating the array (spread)

Bonus: write your own myMap and myFilter without using the built-ins.

Pitfalls: an arrow function with {} but no return inside map gives you an array of undefined · mutating the original object inside map. In React and Vue, not mutating is the law.

Mentor tip: you'll write map, filter, reduce, destructuring, and spread every day in React and Vue. If this week isn't 100% clear, take two extra days.
checklist: I know map vs forEach
I can write a reduce without looking
I know when to use obj.key vs obj[key]
I know spread makes a shallow copy, and what that means
Destructured code doesn't confuse me anymore

12.body:
Task · Expense tracker

  • A form: description, amount, category (food, transport, courses...), date
  • Validation with errors shown in the page, not alert
  • A list of expenses with a delete button each
  • A total that updates automatically
  • Filter by category (select)
  • Everything persists in Local Storage. Refresh and it's still there.

Bonus: an edit button · event delegation: one listener on the list instead of one per button.

Pitfalls: putting user input into innerHTML (someone types <img src=x onerror=alert(1)> and it runs) · treating the DOM as your data. Keep an array in JS as the source of truth and redraw from it. That's exactly what React and Vue do.

Mentor tip: get "data in an array, UI drawn from it" this week and you already understand half of React and Vue.

Task · Modular to-do app

todo-app/
├── index.html
├── css/style.css
└── js/

    ├── storage.js   → save / load

14.body:
Task · Weather app

Use Open-Meteo (free, no API key):

  • Type a city → geocode it → fetch the weather
  • Current temperature, conditions, humidity, wind, and a 7-day forecast
  • Three clear states: loading (spinner), error (city not found / offline), success
  • async / await + try / catch only, no .then
  • Remember the last city in Local Storage

Bonus: a "my location" button with navigator.geolocation · debounce the input (wait 500 ms after typing stops).

Pitfalls: a missing await, so you get Promise {<pending>} · no error handling (networks fail, APIs go down, users typo) · no loading state, so users click 10 times.

Mentor tip: async trips up everyone. Watch the event loop videos twice and draw it on paper. It clicks.

15.body:
Task · Quiz app with classes

A JavaScript quiz with questions you write:

  • class Question: text, choices, answer, isCorrect(answer)
  • class Quiz: questions, current index, score, next(), answer(), isFinished()
  • class QuizUI: rendering only
  • A 15-second timer per question, built with a closure
  • A results screen showing right and wrong answers
  • High score saved in Local Storage

Bonus: createCounter() returning increment, decrement, getValue, where the count is impossible to reach from outside. A classic interview question.

Pitfalls: memorizing the closure definition without being able to write one · god classes. One class, one job.

Mentor tip: every frontend interview asks about closures, this, and the event loop. Come back to this week before every interview.

16.body:
Task · Move the weather app to Vite + PRs

  1. New Vite project (vanilla JS); move your week 14 weather app in
  2. Split it into modules
  3. Install and use an npm package (e.g. dayjs for dates)
  4. Set up ESLint and Prettier
  5. All work on branches (feature/vite-setup, feature/forecast...), each merged through a pull request with a description
  6. Auto-deploy to Vercel or Netlify on every push to main

Submit the repo (3+ PRs visible) and the live link.

Bonus: finish the Main levels of Learn Git Branching · create a merge conflict on purpose and resolve it.

Pitfalls: committing node_modules · API keys in code (use .env and .gitignore it; and remember nothing in frontend code is truly secret) · working directly on main.

Mentor tip: day one at any company: "here's the repo, make a branch, open a PR." People who can do that on day one stand out.

Task · Movies app

If your Project 2 was a movies app, rebuild it in React. Otherwise build one now with TMDB or DummyJSON:

I clean up timers and listeners in onUnmounted

22-vue.title: Vue Router

fields.label: Goal
fields.html: build a multi-page app with no full page reloads.

fields.label: Topics
fields.html: SPA · routes, RouterLink, RouterView · hash vs history mode · router.push / replace / go · dynamic routes, params & query · nested routes · 404 page · navigation guards (beforeEach) · useRouter & useRoute

fields.label: Also watch
fields.html: Router & Route in Composition API · 7 min

fields.label: Read
fields.html: Vue Router guide

22-vue.body:
Task · Multi-page app

Extend your movies app (or start fresh):

  • / home · /movies list with search & filter in the URL (?q=batman&genre=action) · /movies/:id details · /favorites
  • /login (fake) · /profile protected by a navigation guard, redirects to /login
  • A proper 404 page
  • A shared layout; the active RouterLink is styled (router-link-active)

Refresh on /movies/5 after deploying gives a 404? Look up "SPA redirect rules" for Netlify or Vercel.

Bonus: lazy-load pages with component: () => import('./views/MovieDetails.vue') and watch each one load separately in the Network tab.

Pitfalls: going from /movies/1 to /movies/2 reuses the component. If you only fetch in onMounted, the data won't update. Watch the param.

Mentor tip: the URL is the web's oldest and best state manager. Anything a user might share (search, filters, page) belongs in it.
checklist: I know <a> vs <RouterLink>
I know useRouter vs useRoute
I know params vs query
I can write a navigation guard
I know hash vs history mode and why history needs server config

23-vue.title: Styling & Component Libraries

fields.label: Goal
fields.html: know the ways to style Vue, and use a component library wisely.

fields.label: Topics
fields.html: scoped styles & lang · CSS Modules in Vue · Tailwind with Vue · what component libraries are and when to use one · PrimeVue, shadcn-vue, Nuxt UI · icons · <Teleport>

fields.label: Read
fields.html: Tailwind with Vite (same as week 7) · shadcn-vue or PrimeVue: pick one, read its intro & install

23-vue.body:
Task · Mini UI kit

A "Component Gallery" page with Tailwind + your chosen library:

  • BaseButton (variants, sizes, loading) · BaseInput with label, error, v-model · BaseCard with header / default / footer slots · BaseModal (<Teleport>) · Toast · Tabs · Dropdown Menu
  • All support dark mode
  • Then swap them into your movies app

Bonus: a useToast() composable: toast.success("Saved") from any component.

Pitfalls: several component libraries in one project · a library you can't customize.

Mentor tip: at work you'll rarely build a modal or dropdown from scratch (their accessibility is hard). But build one once, so you know what the library does for you.
checklist: I know what scoped does under the hood
I know what problem <Teleport> solves
I know a library like PrimeVue vs shadcn-vue, which copies code into your project
My components work with the keyboard (Tab, Enter, Escape)

24-vue.title: Pinia

fields.label: Goal
fields.html: manage shared state in a large app with Vue's official store.

fields.label: Topics
fields.html: when props and provide / inject aren't enough · what a store is · defineStore: state, getters, actions · setup stores (Composition style) · storeToRefs · Pinia DevTools · client vs server state

fields.label: Read
fields.html: Pinia intro (short; see the setup store example) · Core concepts

24-vue.body:
The course uses options stores (state, getters, actions). Try them, then rewrite the same store as a setup store (ref, computed, functions); it matches everything else you've learned.

Task · Shopping cart

A small store on DummyJSON products:

  • Products, product details, and cart pages
  • useCartStore: add, remove, quantity, total (getter), coupon discount
  • useUiStore: sidebar open/closed, theme
  • Cart persists in Local Storage
  • Cart icon in the navbar shows the item count

Bonus: a small Pinia plugin that persists any store to Local Storage automatically.

Pitfalls: everything in Pinia (form input state belongs in a component ref) · const { count } = useStore() without storeToRefs · API data in Pinia. That's server state: next week.

Mentor tip: Pinia is Vue's official store and replaced Vuex. A course or project using Vuex is outdated.
checklist: I know when I need Pinia and when I don't
I know options stores vs setup stores
I know why storeToRefs is needed for destructuring state
I can watch the store change in Vue DevTools

25-vue.title: TanStack Query

fields.label: Goal
fields.html: handle server data professionally: caching, refetching, mutations.

fields.label: Topics
fields.html: server vs client state · why onMounted + fetch doesn't scale · useQuery, query keys, staleTime, caching · DevTools · dependent & enabled queries · pagination · useMutation & invalidation · optimistic updates

fields.label: Main read
fields.html: TanStack Query for Vue: Overview, Quick Start, Queries, Mutations, Query Invalidation

25-vue.body:
There's no Arabic course for Vue Query specifically. The Arabic course is in React, but the concepts are identical (keys, staleTime, caching, mutations, invalidation) and the API is nearly the same (useQuery({ queryKey, queryFn })). Watch for concepts, write Vue from the docs.

Task · Admin dashboard

Manage products or posts on DummyJSON:

  • A table with pagination and search
  • A details page per item
  • Add, edit, delete with useMutation
  • The table refreshes after changes (invalidateQueries)
  • Skeleton loading instead of spinners
  • Not one onMounted fetch in the whole project

Bonus: optimistic delete: the row disappears instantly and comes back with an error if the request fails.

Pitfalls: putting page.value in the key instead of the ref (or a getter), so the query never updates · copying query data into another ref.

Mentor tip: after TanStack Query you won't write fetches in onMounted again. It shows in code review.
checklist: I know server state vs client state
I know staleTime vs gcTime
I can make a query refetch when a ref changes (reactive query key)
I can run a mutation and refresh data after it

26-vue.title: Testing

fields.label: Goal
fields.html: write tests that prove your code works and catch what breaks when you change it later.

fields.label: Topics
fields.html: why test · unit, integration, E2E · Vitest: describe, it, expect, matchers · Vue Test Utils & Testing Library for Vue · testing Pinia stores · async tests · mocking

fields.label: Start here
fields.html: Testing · vuejs.org (the whole picture)

fields.label: Read
fields.html: Vitest guide · Vue Test Utils · Vue Testing Library · Playwright (for the bonus)

26-vue.body:
The Arabic videos use React and Jest, but the first five cover testing concepts that apply everywhere. Vitest code looks almost exactly like Jest.

Task · Test the cart

On your week 24 shopping cart:

  • Unit tests for the cart store: add, remove, quantity, total, coupon (5+, use setActivePinia(createPinia()))
  • Unit tests for utilities (e.g. price formatting)
  • Component tests: ProductCard shows name and price and "Add to Cart" emits or calls the store · CartPage shows an empty state and the correct total
  • At least one test with a mocked API
  • npm run test:unit all green

Submit the repo and a screenshot of the test results.

Bonus: one Playwright E2E test: open the site, add a product, open the cart, check it's there.

Pitfalls: testing implementation (internal ref names) · tests that always pass. Break the code on purpose: does the test fail?

Mentor tip: you don't need 100% coverage. Start with what would hurt most if it broke: calculations, cart, auth.
checklist: I know unit vs integration vs E2E
I can test a Pinia store on its own
I can assert that a component emitted an event
I can mock a function and assert it was called
My tests check what users see, not implementation details

27-vue.title: Performance & Accessibility

fields.label: Goal
fields.html: make your app fast, and usable by everyone.

fields.label: Performance
fields.html: how Vue tracks changes & re-renders · Vue DevTools performance · v-once, v-memo, shallowRef · computed vs method · lazy routes & defineAsyncComponent · Core Web Vitals (LCP, INP, CLS) · Lighthouse · images & bundle size

fields.label: Accessibility
fields.html: semantic HTML in Vue · keyboard & focus management (especially on route change) · ARIA (and when not to use it) · contrast · screen readers

fields.label: Read
fields.html: Performance · vuejs.org · Accessibility · vuejs.org · Learn Performance · Web Vitals · Learn Accessibility

fields.label: Tools
fields.html: Lighthouse · WAVE

27-vue.body:
Task · Audit & improve

On your biggest project from this level:

  1. Run Lighthouse (mobile) and save a before screenshot
  2. Use Vue DevTools to find components rendering too often
  3. Lazy-load pages
  4. Optimize images
  5. a11y: use the app keyboard-only and fix what breaks; run WAVE and fix its errors
  6. Save an after screenshot
  7. In the README, a table: problem → fix → before / after

Bonus: use your app with a screen reader (NVDA, VoiceOver, or TalkBack) for 5 minutes with your eyes closed. Write down how it felt.

Pitfalls: optimizing without measuring · <div @click> instead of <button>.

Mentor tip: measure before you optimize. Most beginner performance problems are huge images and code that loads before it's needed, not the framework.
checklist: I know how Vue decides a component needs to update
I know when shallowRef helps (big data you won't mutate deeply)
I know what LCP, INP, and CLS mean
I can read a Lighthouse report and know where to start
My app works fully with the keyboard
I know "no ARIA is better than bad ARIA"

28-vue.title: Nuxt: Basics & Routing

fields.label: Goal
fields.html: understand what Nuxt adds to Vue and build pages with file-based routing.

fields.label: Topics
fields.html: what a meta-framework is · CSR vs SSR vs SSG · setup & directory structure · pages & routes · dynamic routes · layouts & components · auto-imports · NuxtLink · assets

fields.label: Read
fields.html: Nuxt intro, then Installation, Directory Structure, Routing

28-vue.body:
The course uses Nuxt 3; current is Nuxt 4. The main difference: app code now lives in app/ (app/pages/ instead of pages/). Most else is the same. When something differs, trust the docs.

Task · A blog in Nuxt

Start a blog (you'll finish it next week):

  • / latest posts · /blog all posts · /blog/[slug] a post · /about
  • A default layout with navbar and footer, a blog layout with a sidebar
  • Posts in data.ts for now
  • TypeScript + Tailwind

Bonus: write posts as Markdown with Nuxt Content.

Pitfalls: setting up vue-router by hand (Nuxt does it from pages) · touching window or localStorage anywhere. Code runs on the server first; use them inside onMounted or <ClientOnly>.

Mentor tip: Nuxt feels like magic at first (auto-imports and more). Read Directory Structure in the docs and you'll see where everything comes from.
checklist: I know CSR vs SSR vs SSG and when each fits
I know how files become routes in Nuxt
I know what auto-imports are and why I don't import ref or components
I can build a dynamic route and read its params

29-vue.title: Nuxt: Data, SEO & Deploy + AI Workflow

fields.label: Goal
fields.html: finish the blog with real data and SEO, ship it, and learn to use AI as a real work tool.

fields.label: Nuxt
fields.html: useFetch & useAsyncData · server routes (server/api/) · SEO & meta (useSeoMeta, useHead) · transitions · plugins & modules · error page · middleware · useCookie & useState · deploy

fields.label: AI workflow
fields.html: prompts with context, constraints, and a precise ask · AI for boilerplate, tests, explanations, reviews · reviewing AI code: never accept what you don't understand · common AI failures: outdated APIs (Vue 2, Options API, Nuxt 2), packages that don't exist, overcomplicated solutions

fields.label: Read
fields.html: Nuxt docs: Data Fetching, SEO and Meta, Deployment · GitHub Copilot docs

29-vue.body:
Task · Ship the blog

  • Posts from an API (e.g. DummyJSON posts) with useFetch
  • At least one server route (server/api/...)
  • SEO: useSeoMeta on every page; dynamic meta on posts
  • A custom error.vue
  • /dashboard protected by route middleware
  • Page transitions
  • Deployed on Vercel or Netlify, Lighthouse SEO & Performance 90+

AI task: use any AI tool to (1) write tests for one component, (2) review one of your files, (3) explain a Nuxt concept you didn't get. In AI_LOG.md, record the exact prompt, the answer, and what was wrong or needed fixing.

Submit the repo, live link, and AI_LOG.md.

Pitfalls: $fetch in setup instead of useFetch (one request on the server, another on the client) · asking AI to "build me a Nuxt blog" with no context gets you Nuxt 2 or the Options API. Give it the version, the API style, the file, and the exact ask.

Mentor tip: AI won't take your job. A developer who uses AI well might. The difference is catching its mistakes, which takes the fundamentals you spent 28 weeks building.
checklist: I know useFetch vs $fetch, and why bare $fetch in setup can request twice
I know where code runs: server, client, or both
I can write a server route
I can generate dynamic SEO meta
I deployed a Nuxt app
I can review AI-written code and catch its mistakes

30-vue.title: Graduation Project
30-vue.body:
Goal: build the strongest piece in your portfolio.

Idea Scope
E-commerce Products, filters, search, cart, mock checkout, orders
Admin dashboard Charts, sortable / filterable / paginated tables, full CRUD, dark mode
Learning platform Courses, lessons, progress tracking, quizzes
Job board Jobs, filters, company pages, saved jobs, applications
CIS event platform Events, registration, QR tickets, admin panel
Your idea Pitch it to your mentor first
Requirement Details
Stack Nuxt or Vue + Vite, TypeScript, Tailwind
Pages 5+, including dynamic routes
State Pinia for client state; TanStack Query (or useFetch in Nuxt) for server state
Auth Login & register (mock or DummyJSON), protected routes
Forms At least one complex validated form
Testing 10+ tests (unit + component)
Performance Lighthouse 90+ in all four
Accessibility Fully keyboard-usable
Responsive Mobile first
Git Branches, PRs, clear commits
Deploy Live on Vercel or Netlify
README Screenshots or GIF, live link, stack & why, setup, challenges, what's next

Submit the repo, live link, and a 2-3 minute demo video.

Mentor tip: one finished, polished project beats ten tutorial clones. Interviewers will open it and ask "why did you do it this way?" everywhere. Know every answer.
checklist: I can build a full Vue or Nuxt app from scratch on my own
TypeScript feels natural
I pick the right tool for each problem (state, fetching, styling)
I test what matters
I think about performance and accessibility from the start
My GitHub has 3+ big, live projects with proper READMEs
I use AI as a tool and catch its mistakes
